utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can just tell the Court about a different aspect of this problem, yes, we were given this document during the break. Mr. Krgovic talked to the witness about this document so that is not the problem. The problem is of a different nature. We received a list of documents from the Prosecution that they have in relation to all of the defences. This is a document that is signed by the main accused but it also concerns the other co-accused. Especially during the period that my client also was a member of the Crisis Staff. This document was not disclosed to us even though we are in the process of reciprocal disclosure. There are rules, for example, if the Prosecution has certain documents, they are to put them on the table. If we have certain documents, we are to put those documents on the table. I cannot believe that this document was discovered yesterday by the Prosecution in their documentation. I'm asking whether will such a document appear in relation to Mr. Tadic which the Prosecution had in its possession before? Perhaps there will be a document relating to Mr. Simic who has finished with his testimony. Questions relating to this document can be put to the witness. There is no problem with that. But in this way, I'm not -- I'm sure that the Prosecution was in possession of this document before so I think, since this will only get an ID number we will give you our position on this document but we believe that this is not the proper way to introduce such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I found these sometime around 5.00 last night. I had -- I had someone read a summary of them because I can't read B/C/S. I served them on Defence counsel this morning. They showed them to their -- they showed them to this witness and I was told that there was no objection and I find it very odd that 50 minutes later, in the middle of testimony, that suddenly there is an objection. However, these are not exculpatory documents, these are referred to -- the second document is referred to within the statement of the witness, and I'm just asking for ID because I have no English translation at the time and I was going to have him read it out because I don't have a full English translation. I've just got a summary last night of what they pertain to. The second one pertains to his being fired or removed by the Crisis Staff, which he indicates he was removed by the executive board. It was the Crisis Staff that removed him on the date that he indicates he was in fact removed in his statement and he was removed by written notice. That's the actual written notice. That's the next document. This document here concerns some orders he's receiving by the Crisis Staff on May 20th and I'm just showing the relationship between this new Crisis Staff and his organisation and himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. This document with ERN number 0061-3077 is not the order dismissing him from office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that this document cannot be discussed with the witness for the simple reason that it's late in the day, the two accused persons have already given their evidence, and we are of the view that it would prejudice their Defence to have this document produced at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Does that include the next document, too, which is referred to in his statement? The notice that he's being fired? Because the statement is incorrect. He's got to clarify his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, the one referred to in his statement because he discusses it, in which paragraph is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 14. He says, "I was dismissed from the post of director of Master by the executive committee on 3 June, 1992." He was dismissed by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that one can be referred to the witness because it was discussed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, I'll move on, however both defendants are still here and they can both be recalled to testify concerning that one document, if there was any prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, there has to be an order in the proceedings, Mr. Weiner, and the Prosecution must search for their documents with due diligence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were removed from your position as director of the Master company, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I was not removed from the position of director. I was replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to that, you received a telephone call from Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got into some sort of argument or quarrel with him on the telephone, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: It's not an argument. It was a conversation. Practically, there were two interpretations of one and the same procedure, namely Milan Simic claimed that I am engaged in some type of work in an unauthorised manner or rather that the goods that were in Master are goods that I'm selling without any authorization. However previously I had received authorisation. However, that authorisation was mostly verbal, oral. The president of the executive board called in the directors of companies, the directors of state-owned companies, to a meeting --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: You got into an argument. Didn't you tell him that he could not dismiss you by force? Didn't you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that argument with Milan Simic who was president of the executive board, and your telling him you couldn't be dismissed by force, you received a notice on June 3rd from the Crisis Staff dismissing you from your position as director of the Master company, isn't that correct? Signed by the defendant Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Milan Simic called me to come to the municipality. After the telephone call, I went to the municipality and at the municipality I tried to explain to him the misunderstanding that existed. He told me that it was his assessment that my behaviour was not in keeping with the position of the executive board and that I should therefore leave the company. I tried to explain to him that my behaviour was in keeping with the instructions that I had had until then. He did not accept that. He said to me that I was no longer the director of Master.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you received a document on or about June 3rd, 1992, removing you as the director of Master, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I think that on that day, Milan Simic -- I mean I did not get any letter. He familiarised me with the fact that I was no longer a director. He said that the executive board would pass a decision of its own appointing a new director.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't a decision issued by the Crisis Staff removing or replacing you as director of Master?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Milan Simic made me aware of this and he was president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I'd like to show you a document with the ERN number 00612706. A Crisis Staff -- a Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff document signed by the defendant Blagoje Simic. Sir, could you help us out and could you read that document starting right from the top? Could you read it into the record, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Could the interpreters be given a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They have already been given copies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the SAO Semberija and Majevica, the Serb" -- I beg your pardon -- "the Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac. The Crisis Staff. Number 161-10/92, date the 3rd of July, 1992. The Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac on the basis of Article 3 of the decision on the introduction of a state of war in the territory of the municipality has passed a decision on relieving of duty the director of DD Master from Bosanski Samac. Marko Kuresevic of Bosanski Samac is being relieved of the duty of DP Master. This decision is passed because of the unauthorised trade in goods of the mentioned person against the explicit bans imposed by the organs of authority of the Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac and without appropriate approval from the executive board. This decision shall enter into force on the day it is passed. Copies: The mentioned person, the executive board, the archives of the Crisis Staff, president of the Crisis Staff, signed Dr. Blagoje Simic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sir, after speaking to Milan Simic, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we proceed, I just want to be clear in my mind of the date. Is it 3rd July or 3rd June, 1992 because the interpretation was 3rd July, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir what is the date at the top of the document? Is it --

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: It says the 3rd of July here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after your conversation with Milan Simic, sir, a letter is issued by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could this screen be turned off? Because it -- I find it very disconcerting. It's bad for my eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it all right? Good. Now after speaking to Milan Simic, this decision was issued, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: He gave me this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Milan Simic of the executive board told you you were going to be replaced and then you received a decision from Blagoje Simic replacing you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I got this decision from Milan Simic. After this conversation he gave me this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is Milan Simic gave you this piece of paper which is signed by Dr. Blagoje Simic on behalf of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose name is listed on there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Simic, DR Blagoje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above that it says Crisis Staff president, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that Milan Simic, Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic, who also is going to come into this equation very shortly, all worked together in the government, in the new civilian government of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also after you received this document, and you're told you're going to be replaced, you get arrested by Stevan Todorovic in relation to this situation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us what happened? Because you indicate in your statement that you got arrested by Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I did not state that Stevan Todorovic had arrested me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you got arrested by the police at Stevan Todorovic's orders or request, right after this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document please be placed before this witness? And could it be read? Because in the statement, in the B/C/S, the text is somewhat different from what the Prosecutor said just now. Could it just be put before the witness, please, his statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The B/C/S copy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Rule 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps to move much faster the witness can be directed to the relevant paragraph, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 14, please. I'll read it in English, you tell me if it's the same in B/C/S. "I was dismissed from the post of director of Master by the executive committee on 3 June, 1992. I was called by Milan Simic who told me that I was no longer employed as of the following day. I protested and said that he could not dismiss me by force but I was soon arrested and spent six days in prison. All of this was organised by Stevan Todorovic." Is that what yours says or is it different in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: You asked me whether Stevan Todorovic arrested me and I said that Stevan Todorovic did not arrest me. I said, I stated, that I received information that this had been organised by Stevan Todorovic. To organise and to arrest are two different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, and I corrected that right after. Now, you were arrested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we proceed, could we have this document marked for identification purposes, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D172ID. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, P172ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I was wondering. It's a Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: While we are on this topic and dealing with paragraph 14, just for clarification, both in the B/C/S version and in the English translation, we have found -- we find the date the 3rd of June, 1992 and the letter coming from the Crisis Staff and which our witness here said was handed over to him by Milan Simic is dated the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's wrong. His dismissal from his post by the executive come is wrong and it's -- I don't know. The letter indicates 3rd of July and this says 3rd of June. That could also be wrong too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness is there. He can explain. Just ask him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, your statement says you were dismissed on the 3rd of June. The decision from the Crisis Staff is the 3rd of July. What date do you recall being dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, shortly after this, you were arrested and you were held for six days. Were you told that that arrest was in relation to this removal or replacement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told -- were you given any reason why you arrested at Stevan Todorovic's orders, right after this incident?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: They did not tell me that they had arrested me at Stevan Todorovic's orders but I said that I received this information later that Stevan Todorovic had organised this. However, I was never given any reasons for my arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware that at the time the Crisis Staff dismissed you, Miroslav Tadic was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I was not replaced by the Crisis Staff. I was replaced by Milan Simic and do not repeat what I did not say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have this document from the Crisis Staff dismissing you. My question is were you aware that Miroslav Tadic was a member of the Crisis Staff? That's my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I know that Miroslav Tadic was in the civilian Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also aware that he was a member of the Crisis Staff from April on? April of 1992 on. If you're not, that's fine. Just were you aware?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic has admitted in a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that he was a member of the Crisis Staff. Do you have any reason to doubt the validity of his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that he was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I have no reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, you should be winding up. Actually I allowed you a few minutes because of our discussion at the bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you lived in a residential building in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that the tenants were ethnically mixed in that building?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you've denied distributing white arm bands or ribbons to the non-Serb tenants? You've made that denial in paragraph 11 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that? I did not understand this because two interpreters were working and I didn't find it very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have denied giving out any white arm bands to the non-Serbs in your building.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: In my building, no arm bands were ever given out to anyone. In my statement, I wrote, and stated that in my building, there was a shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll get to that. I'll get to that shortly but you indicated that you never issued white arm bands or white ribbons, isn't that correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your building, which was a newer building, you set up a shelter in the basement, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you put together a list or a roster of persons who entered and exited that shelter at times of shelling, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: It was not a single list, a single roster. People simply wrote down their names of people who were coming into the shelter and leaving the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in addition to this sign-in sheet as this shelter that you had in your building you also gave out white badges for people to use when they entered the shelter, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On every badge, it said, "Shelter, S-35."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have anybody monitoring at the door indicating you can only enter with this white badge, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: These white badges of the shelter did not serve that purpose for somebody being allowed to enter the shelter or to leave it. Everybody was allowed to enter the shelter. The only objective was to prevent someone who had a grenade or some other kind of weapon from entering the shelter. We didn't want something like that to happen in the shelter. We wanted people who were in the shelter to be able to recognise each other. The shelter is quite big. It's a cellar, and there was only proper light in the cellar that I used, and at that time we managed to somehow organise lighting throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no sign on the door saying, "Admission by white badge only"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: No. There were only signs on the building stating that shelter S-35 was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these white badges would prevent anyone from coming in with a weapon or a hand grenade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: No, not from coming in. Anybody could come into the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination? Re-examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kuresevic. I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to the answers that you gave to the Prosecutor. And in relation to the questions that he had put to you. The Prosecutor asked you at the beginning of the examination whether you were aware of the fact that the Serb municipality of Samac had taken power from the democratic government that had been elected before the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. You then said that this was not a takeover. You said that government was being instituted and you said that the municipal authorities did not function the best possible way. Since you were a member of the SDP, that is to say of a party that was a parliamentary party in the municipality and as far as I know you are president of the municipal committee of your party?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I am now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether at that point, at that time, the municipal assembly met?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Which period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before the 16th and 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the assembly, as a rule, met once a month, and at that time, I don't know. Now it meets once a month but at that time as far as I know, the assembly was not meeting because part of the assemblymen who were from the Muslim population and others who were from the Croat population had already established some kind of government in their territory and they did not come. Such an assembly meeting could not be convened because there could not be a quorum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the assembly adopted any decisions in that period?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: If the assembly does not meet, it cannot pass any decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said to the Prosecutor, when you spoke about the difficulties in the economy, you said that there were problems in communicating with the executive board and other organs. How did they function?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: In no way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. I never asked him about any problems in the economy. I never discussed the economy in my cross-examination. And he raised very quickly his -- that he dealt with the executive board. I never got into executive board. I never -- I'm sorry, the issues of his relationship with the economy in any parts of his company in responding to it. In fact when I started that, this Court stopped me because I was going to get into some of that with that document and show the relationship with the different agencies so if I'm prevented from going into it, counsel should be prevented from going into it too. Either that or if he gets into this issue now on redirect can I now. Try and tender that document at that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, yes, you have explained sufficiently. This wasn't part of your cross-examination. Let's hear from Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it wasn't my intention but since the witness mentioned that the municipal authorities were not functioning, my question was: Was the executive board functioning? My question related to the assembly as part of the municipal government, that the Prosecutor discussed. I didn't want to go into any more details about what this relationship was. Since he mentioned in a reply to the Prosecutor that he had contacts with the executive board, I just wanted to know about these contacts with the executive board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, as long as you don't discuss the economy with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuresevic, could you please tell us, did the executive board function before the 16th and 17th of April in the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my discussion with him was the executive board, what concerned that document and concerned Milan Simic and after the takeover by the new Serb municipality and the Crisis Staff. I did not discuss at any point the executive board prior to April 17th. That's a totally new subject. In fact I never questioned him prior to the 17th other than there was a government and he's now gone into the whole history of the assembly prior to April 17th. This is now outside of the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I see the point Mr. Weiner is making. It's related to the period of questioning. And as he says, his questions related to the period after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question. I think the witness provided a sufficient answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuresevic, the Prosecutor presented you with the agreement of Milan Simic and the Prosecution between Biljana Plavsic and the Prosecutor's Office about the admission of guilt and the judgements which were reached based on these plea agreements. I would like to ask you about the cooperation between the JNA and the SDS. You answered the Prosecutor regarding these questions. Now I would like to ask you whether you as a member of the 4th Detachment, a member of the JNA, do you have any direct knowledge about cooperation with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I think I explained that as well. The 4th Detachment was a military structure and to the extent that -- I don't know such details. To the extent that political parties usually cooperated and talked with the military, that was the extent of the cooperation of our military command with them. I personally didn't have such a need, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As commander of a company in the 4th Detachment, did you or your commander receive any orders or instructions from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I mean, I wasn't the commander as company commander. I didn't receive any instructions from the SDS. As a rule, the army never receives orders or instructions from a political party, from one political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you responded to a question about your arrest and you said that -- you said who organised your arrest. Who actually arrested you? Which body? Which police?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: The military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the prison in Pelagicevo. It was a prison where there were two rooms that were linked together and they were practically Serbs and Croats and Muslims there all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the military police, you mean the military police of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, was there -- did the Army of Republika Srpska exist? This is June.

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says. Yes. Probably this relates to how I got the idea that Stevan Todorovic could have organised something like that, where I got this information from. It's in that period. At the command, there was some bad people. The military police had some bad people who were its members, and according to my deep feelings and conviction, they were not a real, proper army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with Stevan Todorovic before this arrest? Did he bring you into the police station?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before my arrest, Stevan Todorovic met me in passing one day. I was driving in my car towards the medical centre and he was coming from the medical centre. He flashed his lights indicating that I should stop and I stopped. He told me that I should go with him for a talk because there were some problems, there were some objections, remarks, about my conduct. I said, "when would you like to talk?" And he said, "whenever you can." And I said, "well, I have to take this sick person to the hospital and I will come right back." So I did go back. I went to the police station. Do I need to tell this story, these details?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a conflict with Stevan Todorovic and those people who were there, only that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO KURESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a disagreement with them. The people who were around him were pointing a rifle at my forehead, placed a pistol in my mouth. They said I was a Commie, that I sang the song, Tito Party, and so on. Mainly all those people who were around him were not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kuresevic. It's not necessary for to you go on. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuresevic, for giving evidence to the Trial Chamber. We are finished with you. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we can take our break now and have the next witness after the break at 12.50 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are proceeding with the next witness. The Trial Chamber is informed that Mr. Lukic wishes to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have prepared now, in accordance with your instructions a completely redacted statement by Mr. Tubakovic. This is D184/3ID but Your Honours in your instruction for this witness, you said that he would testify for 40 minutes viva voce and 40 minutes would be given for the cross-examination and you said that he would testify in that part in closed session, in view of the fact that these paragraphs that I will question him on refer to a protected witness. I would suggest that in that part where I question the witness, he testifies in private session, because it refers -- it relates to the paragraphs which refer to a protected witness, so perhaps we could move to a completely closed session. Because your instruction, Your Honour Judge Mumba, I don't know what the day was when you decided on that testimony, but on page 86 of the working transcript, it says, let me just find it, you said -- this is page 87, line 9, [In English] "Give viva voce testimony in closed session for 40 minutes, dealing with the matters raised in those paragraphs which are struck off."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because it seems to be the case that this statement was admitted, was going to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it's understood it will be closed session -- I mean it will be private session for the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. That's what I meant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My understanding was that it was under seal that the extent that it named a witness who gave testimony in closed session, only that part of it was. The balance of it wasn't. I think there were only a couple of lines there which actually mentioned someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think let's be clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paragraphs are redacted now. And if he testifies in a private session, then perhaps I believe that there will be no reason for his statement to be under seal, although I'm not sure whether the identity of the space can be determined based on the other paragraphs. Perhaps because of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. As much as possible, proceedings should be in open session. So the statement as redacted will be open, it will be in the public domain, and the paragraphs on which he's supposed to -- his testimony will be in private session because of the concerns regarding the events discussed in those paragraphs that were struck out. So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we clarify but when Your Honour said private session is that only for the testimony in relation to a closed session witness, otherwise it's not in private session? I won't be asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. It's open session, the redacted statement is in the -- is a public one. However, the viva voce testimony of the witness will be held in private session because of the intertwine with matters discussing witnesses who are protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When it comes to cross-examination, I may not even refer to that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, if you don't, then it will be public.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, could approach it on that basis as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic? The witness can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I am questioning the witness on this topic any way and when I start on that topic I will ask for a private session, and then after that, when I am finished we can continue in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, for the transcript, could you please tell us your name, your first name and your last name?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am Djordje Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, I have already explained to you when you were preparing to testify that your written statement, which you signed on the 18th of February of this year, has already been admitted into evidence and that certain parts of that statement have been redacted, and I am going to be questioning you on those parts, the parts which refer to a certain incident about which you have already spoken in writing. And that is why I would like to move to a private session while we are talking about that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, the Trial Chamber is aware of your statement and so is the Office of the Prosecutor, that you started working yet again, if I can put it that way, in the Secretariat for National Defence, from April 1992 and that you worked there until 1993 when you moved to Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, you worked at the Secretariat for National Defence in Samac, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I retired in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of that is in your statement so we are not going to go into all the details.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please be asked to speak into the microphone? The interpreters can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you move nearer the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, was there a so-called communication centre attached to the Secretariat for Defence before the war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, while you worked in the Secretariat so now we are interested in the period from the end of April, and the period after that while you were there, I mean, do you know whether Miroslav Tadic came there and why?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. He came to the communications centre and he spoke to people there from Odzak. He talked about the exchange of these civilians who had been detained in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any details related to these conversations, what did they discuss specifically, who did he talk to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that this was Miro [as interpreted] Matanovic on the other side from Odzak talking to him, and I think Marko Bozanovic too. I think he was also there on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One second, if we can have one small correction in the transcript here on page 86, line 19 it says Miro Matanovic and it was Mijo, because there is also other persons with this name Matanovic. So just avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It should be Mijo Matanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination, the Prosecution? Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, my name is David Re. I'm with the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you some questions about your testimony, and your statement. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you hear me quite clearly?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement which is in evidence here, you speak quite highly of Mr. Miroslav Tadic who is seated in this Court. You've known him for a long time. Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We've known each other for a long time and we were good friends, and I believe that we shall be so in the future too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you related to him?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the defendant or the accused Mr. Simo Zaric? Do you know Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know him, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you known him for?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've known him shorter than I've known Mr. Tadic because he came to Samac later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like Mr. Tadic, is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zaric is my neighbour, we live in the same building, except that his is the fourth entrance and mine is the second. We did not actually visit each other very much but we were on good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the third accused over there, Dr. Blagoje Simic? How long have you known him for?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've known him since he turned 18 and when he was supposed to do his military service. Of course he went to do his military service after completing his university studies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a friend of his?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not a personal friend but we are neighbours. He and Mr. Simic live in the same building that I live in. We all know each other. Everybody in Samac knows me and I know everybody in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe my colleague can clarify because here on page 88, line 9 he said he and Mr. Simic live in the same building and he was referring to Mr. Simic so it's not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, Mr. Tubakovic, you said that he and Mr. Simic live in the same building. Do you mean that Mr. Zaric and Mr. Simic live in the same building?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, Mr. Simic, and I live in the same building. I live at the second entrance, Zaric at the fourth entrance, and Mr. Simic at the seventh entrance. The building has eight entrances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you a patient of Dr. Simic's in Bosanski Samac? Or any members of your family a patient of his?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, possibly but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a customer of Mr. Tadic's cafe, Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Milan Simic, who is an accused who has pleaded guilty in this Court? Do you know him and are you a friend of his?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: He's my friend least of all, but I do know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say friend least of all, do you mean that he's a long-term acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know his father better, because he worked in the same institution practically as I did, namely the municipality. I know Milan too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What about Stevan Todorovic? Do you know him as well?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was my friend least of all. We just said hello to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you related to Marko Tubakovic, who was in the JNA and VRS in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Tubakovic and I are brothers. He is two years younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He of course is one of the gentlemen who signed that report in December, 1992, about the activities in Bosanski Samac committed by the paramilitaries and the Crisis Staff, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of a political party in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I am not, even nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of the SDS, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was a member of the League of Communists, and when that organisation ceased to function, then I was no longer a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your brother Marko Tubakovic never tell you that he had -- he and 12 other members of the military command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade had prepared a report in December, 1992, in relation to the activities of the Crisis Staff, War Presidency, and the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, because the witness already said that he did not know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He was being asked whether his brother had told him anything about it. So the question is okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He did not say this to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you telling the Trial Chamber that until this day, you're unaware that he and Mr. Simo Zaric seated over there signed a report prepared by 11 others, members of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, severely criticising murders, looting, assaults, isolation of Croats, and Muslims, and the activities of the paramilitaries and the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac in 1992? Are you telling the Trial Chamber that until this moment, you were unaware of that document or the fact that your brother co-signed that -- a lengthy report on those matters?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I really did not hear about this particular information because I wasn't interested in it. Let me also say that until the present day, actually I heard that my brother was in Belgrade and why he went to Belgrade, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said you weren't interested in that information. Are you saying that you weren't interested in what the military was doing, the military activities in the Bosanski Samac area in 1992? Is that your evidence, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I say that I know what I did, as far as the military is concerned. As for this information that the command wrote, that is something I really was not interested in because it did not fall within the area of my own work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you had a specific role in relation to the formation of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, sir, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I carried out the mobilisation of military conscripts for that brigade. On the basis of the allotments we were given, we sent soldiers to units. This was the job of the particular organ or authority where I had spent my entire career or rather where I ended my career.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, you worked on forming a Special Battalion in Samac which was with other units from which grew the 2nd Posavina Brigade and you worked on that task until February of 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course in working on those tasks, that is, the formation of a Special Battalion which was going to be part of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, you would have had to have contact with the command of the 2nd Posavina brigade, including your brother, wouldn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any contact with my brother. He was involved in operational work. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll go back to my question. My question concerned the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Take your brother out. In doing your job in 1993 in forming a Special Battalion which was to be part of the 2nd Posavina brigade, you had to have contact or you had contact with the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The establishment of a Special Battalion or rather the 2nd Posavina Brigade went through lower level units. So the command, the real command, did not really go into the response of mobilised persons which was my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, are you saying that in doing your job, forming a Special Battalion that was to be part of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, you had no contact with members of the command, plural, of the 2nd Posavina Brigade? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I had contact with the command of that Special Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now the Special Battalion that was formed of Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: This Special Battalion was formed out of all units or rather members of previously established units, in which there were people of other ethnic backgrounds as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What percentage, sir? You formed the battalion. What percentage were non-Serbs in this Special Battalion you formed between April, 1992 and February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking 1, 2, 3 per cent perhaps? That small?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: That small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of this Special Battalion, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander was Milan Josic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he from Serbia or was he a local?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a local man from Obudovac, the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Special Battalion, did it contain any members of the Serbian specials or paramilitaries who came into the town just before the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: These specials were not there. This was an army setup from units in the territory of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were units which were in the 4th Detachment or the JNA prior to May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: These are members of all other units which had been established in peace time in the territory of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's yes, is it? The JNA and 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: These who were in the previous units, the previous wartime units, that means before the war, that was the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as part of your job of what you say in your statement as specifically working on manning a Special Battalion that was formed from conscripts domiciled in Samac and other units being formed and growing into the 2nd Posavina Brigade -- do you have a copy of your statement then, sir? Can he please be provided with a copy of his statement, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask for the B/C/S version of the document to be placed before the witness. P184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that he then be shown the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, please turn to paragraph 18 of your statement. I don't want to you read it. I just want you to have it there in case we need to refer to it. Paragraph 18. Now, sir, I want to ask you a question, please. My question is, as part of your job in specifically working on manning this Special Battalion which was formed from conscripts in the Samac municipality, did you have to arrange for things such as weapons, equipment, uniforms and those things?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were obliged only to bring people to the assembly point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence, to be quite clear on this, is that these people from the former JNA were transformed into the 2nd Posavina Brigade which was part of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once it was transformed into the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. All reserves of the Yugoslav People's Army, which were filled by my municipality, these were all the reserve forces, this was not the active component of the JNA. These were the reserves so when the war broke out we mobilised those people. They were civilians who were performing their own work, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war broke out, were they mobilised into the JNA or into the VRS, sir? You said you started working there on the 28th of April. What were they mobilised into?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Into the Serbian army primarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of the 28th of April, 1992, they were being mobilised into the Serbian army, were they?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there were other ethnic groups within that army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you've already said that, but I'm not asking you about that. And when they were mobilised into the Serbian army from the 28th of April, 1992, they were of course given JNA weapons, equipment, and uniforms, and housed in JNA barracks when necessary, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: They were not placed in the barracks at the time because there was no military barracks in the municipality of Samac at the time. They were brought to the assembly point and they were given their clothing and weapons but I wasn't present on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware that they were given JNA weapons, equipment and uniforms, weren't they? Because there was no where else they could have got them from on the 28th -- from the 28th of April, 1992, was there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement you also refer to telephones working or not working. The situation was, in 1992, after the military takeover in Samac on the 17th of April, that there were some telephones working in the municipality, specifically there were telephones working in the SUP, civilian protection, the municipal building and the Crisis Staff, weren't there, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, the telephones functioned everywhere in the first couple of days. They were not cut off. There was no need for that. We had electricity. Later, when the telephone service was cut, my municipal secretariat didn't have phone service. We had to use radios.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: To communicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you said, "the telephones were out of operation for all citizens and it is out of the question that lines were cut selectively." That's in paragraph 23. I'm suggesting to you there were some telephones working when in the time you say all the telephones weren't working specifically in the SUP, the Crisis Staff, the municipal building and the civilian protection. If you don't know, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if they had them there. I didn't have them. I had to go to Bijeljina in order to deal with my own affairs because there was no phone service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you say you don't know, will you correct your statement where you said it was out of operation for all citizens? Now that you've admitted to the Trial Chamber that you just don't know? Will you now correct your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I object to a question put in this way. In his statement, the witness clearly said that this referred to telephones for citizens, for physical persons. He did not talk about phones at social or legal entities, and that is why, that is why he said that according to his knowledge, there were no phones for everybody equally but he was thinking only of physical persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. My learned friend again is cluing a witness, putting -- telling the witness the basis of the objection and it's actually incorrect. The statement says: "There were no telephone lines for a long time and I know that myself because I wanted to send a fax in connection with the work myself. I had to go to Bijeljina and send it from then. The telephones were out of operation for all citizens, and it is out of the question the lines were cut selectively." I object on two bases. One my learned friend telling the witness what he was thinking, and secondly, misquoting the statement. The statement clearly says that telephone lines were not working in Samac, and he in his work had to go somewhere else. It's fairy outrageous in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's about the opposite actually, through questions like there, the Prosecution is trying to impose an answer to the witness compared to what he said in his statement. If the Prosecutor wishes to did such a question of the witness he first should ask him whether he knew whether citizens had their phones switched off. The question of whether the telephones were working in certain places is something that the Prosecution is using to confuse the witness. And in such a way, is trying to get him to change his statement. The witness quite clearly said whose telephones were cut. The witness clearly said something in his statement and now the Prosecution is trying to get him to say something else and is twisting his words, not checking what he actually meant when he said that in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness can answer whether he knows or doesn't know whether his statement is wrong but I wish to place on the record the Prosecution's objection to the objections we get all the time on the basis that we are "attempting to confuse" witnesses. The Prosecution has no desire to confuse witnesses. We want clear evidence, whether it is in favour of our case or contrary to our case. We want what they say to be clear. We have no forensic purpose whatsoever in attempting to confuse witnesses. That would be the amateur hour for advocacy as far as the Prosecution is concerned. Those continual objections appear to be designed to prevent the Prosecution from putting matters which are in its case. There is no objection I know of known to the law of confusing the witness. In cross-examination, we are entitled to put to the witnesses our case and to put to the witness a conflict between his previous statement and what he's given in evidence. So we object strongly to this continual objection of "confusing". It is not happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In some cases, it does happen that the witness -- matters are put to the witness which are not clear by the Prosecution. Sometimes questions are loaded but in this particular case, the witness, the question by the Prosecution was quite clear and the witness, who is supposed to know what was happening at the relevant time and who has also given evidence through his statement, should be able to answer and clarify what he meant to say in his statement. Because the statement does say that the telephones were out of operation for all citizens. Prior to that he does explain how he himself had a problem getting the services he needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all of us in these proceedings, which have been following the proceedings so far know what's happened with the telephones in Samac. This is something that should be of interest to the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber, and he said that. When we are talking about selective cuts, in this way, however, the Prosecution is trying to get the witness to back down from what he said. The Prosecutor should be interested whether phones were selectively cut to Muslims and Croats. If this is what he's interested in, why doesn't he ask the witness? Instead of trying to get the witness to change his statement. This is the misleading of the witness. Here we are interested in specific facts which are relevant to these proceedings. This is what the witness said in his statement, what the Prosecution stated during their case in chief, and this is something that they are not actually putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think it's a difference in the style of cross-examination because in spite of what a witness may state, if the Prosecution or the opposing party have instructions to the contrary, they have the right to put the contrary instructions to the particular witness and it's up to the witness to give an answer according to what he knows. If he knows as a factual statement as to what he stated, he cannot change his answer and agree with the Prosecution. He can still insist on what is stated in his evidence. So the Prosecution is entitled to put a statement contrary to what the witness has said in his statement so that the witness can answer according to what he knows. He may change his testimony and that is part of the process of cross-examination. It's also to test whether or not the witness is telling the truth, in which case he will be consistent. If he is not, then he's prone to change his testimony. We will adjourn now and continue our proceedings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
